section_title: Why should our ordinary word be trustworthy?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 12 Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath. Simply let your “Yes” be yes, and your “No,” no, so that you will not fall under judgment.

context_lines: James returns to speech, warning against swearing by heaven, earth or another oath. The positive instruction is simple: let yes and no be reliable. Truthfulness is to characterize ordinary dealings, not depend on finding a stronger-sounding promise.
The warning about judgment gives the instruction weight. A claim of devotion to God must not coexist with speech that misleads others.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians agree on truthful speech but differ over whether every solemn oath is forbidden. The Reformed [Westminster Confession, 22.1–4](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html), permits lawful oaths in serious matters while rejecting rash or deceptive swearing. The Catholic [Catechism, 2154](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_three/section_two/chapter_one/article_2/ii_taking_the_name_of_the_lord_in_vain.html), likewise permits oaths for grave and right reasons. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-general-epistle-of-st-james/) allows a solemn oath before a magistrate.

The Mennonite Church USA [Confession, article 20](https://www.mennoniteusa.org/who-are-mennonites/what-we-believe/confession-of-faith/truth/), instead calls for avoiding oaths, including affirming the truth in legal matters without swearing. Its reading applies James’ instruction directly to both ordinary speech and formal assurances.
god_plan_lines: This closely parallels Jesus’ teaching in [Matthew 5:33–37](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/5.htm). Both direct people toward dependable speech before God. The connection places James’ practical instruction within the way of life Jesus teaches His followers.
